title: The protected passed pawn
summary: A passed pawn defended by another pawn ties down the enemy king, and your own king is free to capture the rest.
part.tied.title: The tied king
part.tied.summary: The enemy king cannot capture the protected pawn or leave its square. Your king goes alone to capture the rest, and the pawn stays put.
part.twoTasks.title: One king, two jobs
part.twoTasks.summary: When the defender has a pawn too, his king looks for the square that defends that pawn without leaving the square of the protected one.
part.twoPassers.title: Two passers on the other side
part.twoPassers.summary: A game from the World Junior: the protected pawn ties the king down, and the free king goes to stop the enemy pawns.
part.base.title: Attacking the base
part.base.summary: If the enemy king goes after the rear pawn, either it leaves the square and the front pawn runs, or it stays inside and your king defends the base in time.
part.kingToPawns.title: The king goes to its pawns
part.kingToPawns.summary: When both sides are going to queen, the king does not chase the enemy pawn: it helps its own, and mate comes first.
part.corner.title: Near the corner
part.corner.summary: Right next to the corner the protected pawn only draws, because of stalemate. With a target on the other side, even a protected rook pawn wins.
part.shadow.title: The king that shadows
part.shadow.summary: When the attacking king cannot reach its target, the defender holds by shadowing it square by square. Here you defend.
part.finish.title: Summary
part.finish.summary: Three rules for your games, how the king finishes the job, and then the whole ending in the practical challenge.
step.t_tied: A position from the manuals of Fine and Benko, slightly reduced. Each side has a king and two pawns, but the c5 pawn is passed and defended by b4; the h5 pawn has no one. What is White's plan, and why can't Black do the same?
step.t_tied.hint1: Can the black king capture the c5 pawn? And can it walk away from it?
step.t_tied.hint2: Count how many moves the white king needs to reach h5, and where the black king would have to be to defend it.
step.square: This is the protected passed pawn. The black king cannot capture c5, because b4 defends it. And it cannot walk away: if it leaves the square of c5, from c5 to f8, the pawn runs and queens. To defend h5 it would have to go to g6, outside the square. The black king is tied down; my king is tied to nothing.
step.d_tied: The white king goes via f4, g3 and h4; the c-pawn does not move.
step.d_tied.m1: 1.Kf4. The king heads for the kingside, where the target is.
step.d_tied.m2: 1...Kf6, to hold g5. If the black king goes to g6, it leaves the square, and the c-pawn runs.
step.d_tied.m3: 2.Kg3. The road through g4 is closed by the h5 pawn, so I go round via h4.
step.d_tied.m4: 2...Ke5. Black gives up on h5 and comes back near the c-pawn.
step.d_tied.m5: 3.Kh4. The h5 pawn has no defender: the black king, on e5, cannot go to g6 without leaving the square of c5.
step.d_tied.m6: 3...Kd5. The black king can only watch.
step.d_tied.m7: 4.Kxh5. A pawn up, and the protected pawn still ties the black king down. Now it is time to come back and finish.
step.tiedPush: What if White pushed the c-pawn at once? See what happens after 1.c6?, which looks quick. The pawn leaves c5 and b4 no longer defends it. Then 1...Kd6 2.c7 Kxc7: the protected pawn has become a captured pawn. Now the free king is the black one: while my king captures h5, it goes to c4 and captures b4, and the passer that remains is Black's. The protected pawn works standing still.
step.tiedMove: Your turn. Take the king to h5 by the shortest road, without touching the c-pawn.
step.tiedMove.hint: The white king has work on the kingside. Do not touch the c5 pawn: it already does its job standing still.
step.tiedMove.done: That's it. The black king stayed tied to the c5 pawn, and your king captured h5 undisturbed.
step.t_twoTasks: It is the first position, except that the black pawn is on f5, not h5: two files closer to the c-pawn. Can the white king still go and get it?
step.t_twoTasks.hint1: On which squares does the black king defend f5?
step.t_twoTasks.hint2: Are those squares inside the square of c5, from c5 to f8?
step.twoTasksWhy: It does not win. From e6 or f6, the black king defends f5 and stays inside the square of c5. With the pawn on h5 it would have to go to g6, outside the square; with the pawn on f5, one square does both. It is the question of every ending like this: the defending king has two jobs; is there a square that does both?
step.d_twoTasks: The white king tries to go round, and the black king always finds the square that does both jobs.
step.d_twoTasks.m1: 1.Kf4. Attacks f5: the black king must defend it at once, without leaving the square of c5.
step.d_twoTasks.m2: 1...Kf6. Defends f5 and stays inside the square of c5.
step.d_twoTasks.m3: 2.Kg3. The white king goes round, to come in via h4 and g5.
step.d_twoTasks.m4: 2...Ke5. Still defending f5, still inside the square. And it still shuts d4 and f4, the white king's entry squares.
step.d_twoTasks.m5: 3.Kh4. Now the white king threatens 4.Kg5 and capturing f5.
step.d_twoTasks.m6: 3...Kf6, shutting g5. 3...Kf4? would leave the square, and 4.c6 would queen.
step.twoTasksMove: Now you play Black. Your king is on d7, and the white king is going to attack f5. Find the square that does both jobs.
step.twoTasksMove.hint: f5 needs a defender and c5 needs a guard: which square is close to both, without letting the white king get in front?
step.twoTasksMove.done: That's it. Only 1...Ke7 holds. 1...Ke6? looks more active, but loses to 2.Kd4!, and Black, to move, has no good move. 1...Kc6? loses to 2.Kf4.
step.t_jakovenko: Now it is the attacking king that has two jobs. World Junior Championship, Yerevan, 2000. Dmitry Jakovenko, with White, traded rooks and reached this ending against Varuzhan Akobian. The e5 pawn is passed and protected by f4, but on the queenside Black has two pawns, c5 and d5, against one, on c2: a passer can come out of them. Where does the white king go?
step.t_jakovenko.hint1: Can the black king walk away from the e5 pawn?
step.t_jakovenko.hint2: Who is going to stop the c- and d-pawns, if not the white king?
step.jakovenkoWhy: Jakovenko played 46.Kd3! and took his king to the queenside: 46...Kd7 47.Kc3 Kc7 48.Kb3 Kc6 49.Ka4 d4 50.Ka5 Kd5 51.Kb5 c4 52.e6 d3 53.e7, and Akobian resigned. The e5 pawn kept the black king near it; the white king stopped both queenside pawns. With 46.Kf3?, the wrong way, 46...d4! and the white king can no longer catch the pawns: a draw.
step.d_twoPassers: The same idea in a smaller position: two separate black passers, f4 and h5, and the black king tied to the c5 pawn.
step.d_twoPassers.m1: 1.Kf3! Attacks f4 and stays inside the square of h5. 1.Kf2? draws: 1...Ke6, and the black king reaches f5 in time to defend f4 without leaving the square of c5.
step.d_twoPassers.m2: 1...Ke6. Too late: from e6 the black king does not defend f4.
step.d_twoPassers.m3: 2.Kxf4. One passer fewer, and the white king still watches h5.
step.d_twoPassers.m5: 3.Kg3. The road through g4 and g5 is closed; the king goes round via h4.
step.d_twoPassers.m6: 3...Ke6. If 3...Kg6, it leaves the square of c5, and 4.c6 queens.
step.d_twoPassers.m7: 4.Kh4, and h5 falls next move: the black king has no way to defend it.
step.twoPassersMove: Your turn. Find the king square that takes care of both black passers.
step.twoPassersMove.hint: One king, two jobs: attack one pawn without leaving the square of the other.
step.twoPassersMove.done: That's it. From f3 the king attacks f4 and reaches h5.
step.t_base: So far the black king only watched. Now it has reached b4 and attacks the a4 pawn, the base of the protected pawn. Should White worry?
step.t_base.hint1: Look at the square of the b5 pawn. Where is the black king?
step.t_base.hint2: Count: how many moves does the b5 pawn need to queen, and how many does the black king need to reach b8?
step.baseWhy: The black king went after the base and left the square of the front pawn. With 1.b6, the pawn needs two moves to queen, and the black king, from b4, cannot reach b8 in time. Attacking the base of a protected pawn almost always costs the square.
step.d_base.m1: 1.b6. The pawn goes on alone; a4 no longer matters.
step.d_base.m2: 1...Kc5. The king comes back, but the pawn needs two moves to b8, and the king needs three.
step.d_base.m3: 2.b7. The pawn is one step from b8, and the black king is still on the fifth rank.
step.d_base.m4: 2...Kc6. Too late: the king arrives beside the pawn, not in front of it.
step.d_base.m5: 3.b8=Q. The queen is out of the king's reach.
step.d_baseInside: Now the black king attacks the base f3 without leaving the square of e4. Then my king has to defend the base in time. With 1.Kd3?, 1...Kxf3, and both pawns queen: a draw.
step.d_baseInside.m1: 1.Kf2! Defends f3. Black, to move, has no good move: if 1...Ke5, 2.Ke3 and the black king retreats. With the king on f2 and White to move, it would be a draw: here whoever moves loses.
step.d_baseInside.m2: 1...g4, the last try: it attacks the base with the pawn.
step.d_baseInside.m3: 2.fxg4. The base changes place: now the white pawn is on g4.
step.d_baseInside.m4: 2...Kxe4. One pawn each? No: the g-pawn is White's, and Black has none left.
step.d_baseInside.m5: 3.Kg3. The white king escorts the g-pawn to the eighth rank.
step.baseInsideMove: Your turn. The base f3 is under attack. Defend it with the king at the right moment.
step.baseInsideMove.hint: Which square defends f3 and does not let the black king in?
step.baseInsideMove.done: That's it. With 1.Kf2 the base is defended, and the black king, with no good move, has to retreat.
step.t_kingToPawns: So far the king went to capture pawns. Now it cannot catch the enemy pawn. A study published by Chessforall321. The g6 pawn is passed and protected by f5, but Black's h6 pawn is going to run, and the white king is far from it. Where does the white king go?
step.t_kingToPawns.hint1: The white king cannot catch the h-pawn. What can it reach?
step.t_kingToPawns.hint2: With the king on f6 or g6, the f- and g-pawns do what they cannot do alone.
step.kingToPawnsWhy: 1.g7+? looks natural, but the black king captures g7 and Black is the one who wins. The plan is the king: via d6 and e7 to f6, next to the black king. When the h-pawn queens, my pawns will already have mated.
step.d_kingToPawns: The king has reached f6 after 3.Kxf6 h4. Now the pawns.
step.d_kingToPawns.m1: 4.g7. It shuts f8 and h8; the black king only has h7, because my king covers f7.
step.d_kingToPawns.m2: 4...h3. The black king only has h7; Black runs with the pawn to queen.
step.d_kingToPawns.m3: 5.Kg6. The king shuts f7 and h7: the black king has no squares left.
step.d_kingToPawns.m4: 5...h2. Black can only move the pawn.
step.d_kingToPawns.m6: 6...h1=Q. The queen is born one move too late.
step.d_kingToPawns.m7: 7.f7#. Mate: the f-pawn gives check, and the g-pawn and the king shut every square.
step.kingToPawnsMove: Your turn: take the king to f6.
step.kingToPawnsMove.hint: The king goes near the black king, not after the h-pawn.
step.kingToPawnsMove.done: That's it. With the king on f6, the pawns give mate before the black queen arrives.
step.t_corner: So far the protected pawn nearly always won. Now the cases where it does not. The b6 pawn is passed and protected, and the white king is close. Even so, can White win? Look for the danger before looking for the move.
step.t_corner.hint1: The black king has few squares: a8, b8, c8. Count how many are left when the white king comes close.
step.t_corner.hint2: If the black king has no move at all and is not in check, what happens?
step.corner: Here the protected pawn does not win. The black king walks between a8 and b8, and every step of my king takes its last square away: no move and no check is stalemate.
step.d_corner: Watch the white king arrive and find no way in.
step.d_corner.m2: 1...Kb8. In front of the pawn, where it cannot pass.
step.d_corner.m3: 2.Kc6. The white king takes c7 and b7 away from the black king.
step.d_corner.m4: 2...Ka8. The corner: the black king still has b8.
step.d_corner.m5: 3.Kc7, and it is stalemate: the black king has no move and is not in check. 3.b7+ does not work either: 3...Kb8 4.Kb6 is stalemate just the same.
step.rookTargetMove: Now the protected pawn is a rook pawn, a5, defended by b4, and the black king is already in the corner. But the b5 pawn is a target. Take the king there.
step.rookTargetMove.hint: The a5 pawn stays where it is. 1.a6? leaves the protection of b4: 1...Ka7 and 2...Kxa6.
step.rookTargetMove.done: That's it. The a5 pawn stays put and the white king goes to get b5. Near the corner, the protected pawn only draws when the king has nothing to capture.
step.t_shadow: A classic position, which the manuals credit to Walker. Now you defend, with Black, after 1.Kd2. White has the protected passer on b4, defended by c3; the black c4 pawn covers b3 and d3, but nothing defends it. The white king wants to reach d4, e4 or f4. Where must the black king stand?
step.t_shadow.hint1: The white king will try to go round on the kingside.
step.t_shadow.hint2: When the white king is on the third rank, the black one must be on the fifth, on the same file, with White to move.
step.shadowWhy: If the white king steps onto d4, e4 or f4, it captures c4 or gets in, and wins. The black king does not allow it: it stands in front of it, d5 against d3, e5 against e3, f5 against f3. Each white step, one black step. It is what the books call corresponding squares.
step.d_shadow: Watch the black king shadow the white one from the start.
step.d_shadow.m1: 1.Kd2. The white king wants d4, from where it captures c4.
step.d_shadow.m2: 1...Kd5! In front of it: d4 is shut.
step.d_shadow.m3: 2.Ke3. Now the white king tries e4, and from there d4.
step.d_shadow.m4: 2...Ke5! Only this. 2...Kc6? allows 3.Kd4, and c4 falls.
step.d_shadow.m5: 3.Kf3. One more step sideways, towards f4.
step.d_shadow.m6: 3...Kf5! The white king cannot step onto f4.
step.d_shadow.m7: 4.Kg3. The white king goes further, to lure the black one to g5.
step.d_shadow.m8: 4...Ke5! Here it does not follow: on g5 the black king would be far from c4 and d4. From e5 it shuts d4 and f4.
step.d_shadow.m9: 5.Kg4. The white king threatens to come in via f4 or f5.
step.d_shadow.m10: 5...Ke4! Face to face again: f4 and f5 are shut, and c4 is still close.
step.targetMove: Now the black king is on d5 and the white one on d2. Keep the white king away from c4 and d4.
step.targetMove.hint: The white king wants to go to e3. Pick a square from which, after 2.Ke3, you can answer 2...Ke5.
step.targetMove.done: Right. 1...Kc6? and 1...Ke5? lose to 2.Ke3: with the kings on e3 and e5 and Black to move, the black king has to give way. From d6, after 2.Ke3, 2...Ke5 shuts the road with White to move.
step.rules: Three rules. First: the protected passed pawn works standing still; it ties the enemy king to its square, and pushing it early gives it away. Second: your king is the free piece; it captures what is on the other side and stops the enemy passers, looking for the square that does two jobs. Third, for the defender: find the square that defends your pawn without leaving the square, and shadow the enemy king square by square; near the corner, stalemate saves you.
step.d_convert: After the capture, the king comes back, and the protected pawn opens the way to the last black pawn.
step.d_convert.m1: 1.Kd4. The king comes to the centre, near the pawns.
step.d_convert.m2: 1...Kb7. The black king cannot capture c5, which b4 defends, and must stay near b5 and c5.
step.d_convert.m3: 2.Kd5. The white king arrives beside the c-pawn.
step.d_convert.m4: 2...Kc7. In front of the c-pawn: if the black king walks away, the pawn advances.
step.d_convert.m5: 3.c6! The pawn is now defended by the king, and the c5 square is free for me.
step.d_convert.m6: 3...Kc8. The black king cannot capture c6, which my king defends.
step.d_convert.m7: 4.Kc5. Now b5 is attacked and no one defends it.
step.d_convert.m9: 5.Kxb5. Two pawns against none. The black king cannot hold both.
step.recapMove: Now the whole ending, with the white king on f2. Start by taking the king in the right direction.
step.recapMove.hint: The target is on h5. The c5 pawn stays where it is.
step.recapMove.done: That's it. The king heads for h5, and the black king cannot follow it without letting the c-pawn go.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: the whole ending. Capture the h-pawn, come back, and win the b5 pawn.
ex.e17: The b5 pawn is passed and protected by a4. Black has a passed pawn on f4, defended by the king. What is the plan? Find the winning move.
ex.e17.hint: Can the black king defend f4 without leaving the square of the b5 pawn? Try the squares around f4.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Kg4 (1.Ke2, 1.Kf2 and 1.Kg2 also win) and, next move, 2.Kxf4. To hold f4, the black king would have to go to e4 or g3, outside the square of b5, and then the b-pawn runs and queens. 1.b6? is hasty: 1...Kd6 catches the pawn, and the f4 pawn is still alive; it is a draw. The protected pawn works standing still; the king is the one that walks.
ex.e12: The protected passed pawn is a rook pawn, on h5. Does it still win, with the black king away from the corner? Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: The black king may well go to the corner. What decides is that the white king has something to capture: first c7, then g5.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kg2 (1.Kg1 and 1.Kh2 also win), then 2.Kf3 and 3.Ke4, and the king goes after the c7 pawn. 1.h6? loses: 1...Kg6 takes the pawn and Black's c-pawn decides. A protected rook pawn only draws when the defending king is in the corner and the attacking king has nothing to capture; here it has the c-pawn.
ex.e13: White has the protected passed pawn on c5, but Black has a passed pawn too, on d4. Only one move holds.
ex.e13.hint: The black king has two jobs: defend d4 and stay inside the square of the c-pawn. Find the square that does both.
ex.e13.solution: 1...Ke5! defends d4 and stays in the square of c5; after 2.c6, 2...Kd6 (or 2...Ke6) stops the pawn. 1...Ke6? and 1...Kc6? lose to 2.Ke4!, which captures d4. 1...Kc4? loses to 2.c6, and 1...d3? to 2.Ke3, which takes the pawn. The d4 pawn ties the white king just as c5 ties the black one: it is a draw.
ex.e08: The a6 pawn is passed and protected, but Black has two passed pawns, on e4 and h5. Only one move wins.
ex.e08.hint: The black king is tied to the a6 pawn. The white king must stop both black pawns.
ex.e08.solution: 1.Kg3! The king stays close to both pawns: it catches h5 and does not let e4 through. 1.a7? is hasty: the black king takes the pawn and it is a draw. After 1.Kg3, 2.Kf4 goes after the e-pawn.
ex.e14: The f5 pawn is protected, and your passed pawn on b5 is close to the white king. Here every black king move is the only one. Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: The white king is going to capture b5. The black king must be close enough to capture the f-pawn when that happens.
ex.e14.solution: 1...Kd5!, and after 2.Kd3, 2...Ke5!, and after 3.Kc3, 3...Kd5! The black king shadows the white one without leaving the square of f5. One line: 4.Kb4 Kc6, 5.Ka5 Kc5, 6.f6 Kd6, 7.Kxb5 Ke6 and 8...Kxf6, a draw. 1...b4? loses to 2.Kd3, and 1...Kd6? or 1...Kf6? to 2.Kd4. With the pawn on a5, far away, White would win; on b5, close by, the black king gets there in time.
ex.e10: White has a protected passed pawn on a4, but it is a rook pawn and the white king is far away. Only one move holds.
ex.e10.hint: The black king must stay near the a-pawn and, at the same time, be ready to face the white king as it approaches.
ex.e10.solution: 1...Kd6! and, after 2.Kf3, 2...Kd5! With 1...Kc6? White plays 2.Kg3! and arrives in time. After 1...Kd6, if 2.a5, the black king goes to c5 and b6 and captures the a-pawn. The protected rook pawn is the case where the defender is saved most often.
ex.e15: A study published by Chessforall321. The black king attacks g3, the base of the protected passed pawn. Only one move wins.
ex.e15.hint: Once the black king takes g3, both sides will get a queen. What matters is where the white king stands, and whose move it is.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Ke2!, and after 1...h5, 2.Ke3! Now Black is to move and in zugzwang: 2...Kxg3, 3.f5 h4, 4.f6 h3, 5.f7 h2, 6.f8=Q h1=Q and 7.Qg7+ (7.Qf4+, 7.Qg8+ and 7.Qd6+ also win). With the white king on e3, queen and king hunt the black king down to mate or win the queen. 1.Ke3? at once leaves White to move in the same position: 1...h5! and it is a draw. 1.Kg2? also runs into 1...h5! and a draw, and 1.f5? into 1...Kxf5.
ex.e16: A study published by Chessforall321. The h7 pawn is passed and protected by g6, but Black's b4 pawn is going to queen. Only one move wins, and after that every move is the only one. Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: The white king will not catch the b-pawn. Take the king close to the black king: with the g- and h-pawns there is a mate.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kf5! b3 2.Ke6! b2 3.h8=Q+! Kxh8 4.Kf7! b1=Q 5.g7+ Kh7 6.g8=Q+ Kh6 and 7.Qg6 is mate. The white king ignores the b-pawn and goes to f7, where it helps the g-pawn queen with check. 1.Kxe4? loses to 1...b3!, and 1.h8=Q+? at once, 1...Kxh8, loses too: the b-pawn queens first.
key.tied: The protected white pawn ties the black king down beside it. The white king is free to cross to the other side and capture the black pawn. White wins, whoever is to move.
key.twoTasks: The black king has two jobs: defend its own pawn and watch the protected pawn. Here one square does both, and it is a draw.
key.jakovenko: World Junior Championship 2000, Yerevan: Jakovenko let his protected pawn tie down the black king and took his own king to stop the two black pawns. He won.
key.base: The black king went after the rear pawn, the one protecting the passer. But to get there it left the path of the front pawn, which runs through and queens.
key.kingToPawns: The white king does not chase the black pawn: it goes to help its own two pawns, which give mate before the black queen is born.
key.corner: Protected pawn on the sixth rank, right next to the corner: the black king sits in front of it and cannot be driven out without stalemate. A draw.
key.shadow: A classic defence: the black king shadows the white king, always in front of it, and the white king never gets in. A draw.
history: A protected passed pawn is a passed pawn defended by another pawn. The enemy king cannot capture it, and it cannot wander away from it either, or the pawn would queen. In practice it is like having an extra king: your own king is free to go and collect the pawns on the other side of the board. That is why it appears in every endgame book, from Reuben Fine and Pal Benko to Mark Dvoretsky, and Jesús de la Villa lists it among the hundred endgames every player must know. But it does not always win: near the corner, or when there is nothing to capture on the other side, the draw appears, and this lesson shows when.
practice: Now the real ending: the protected c5 pawn, the lonely black g5 pawn, and your king still on e2. Tie the black king down with the pawn, capture the g-pawn and come back. Pick your pace and go.
